Memory-assisted decoder for approximate Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill codes

Kwok Ho Wan Corresponding author: kwok.wan14@imperial.ac.uk Affiliation: Mathematical Physics, Department of Mathematics, Imperial College London, London, SW7 2AZ, UK Affiliation: QOLS, Blackett Laboratory, Imperial College London, London, SW7 2AZ, UK    Alex Neville Affiliation: QOLS, Blackett Laboratory, Imperial College London, London, SW7 2AZ, UK    Steve Kolthammer Affiliation: QOLS, Blackett Laboratory, Imperial College London, London, SW7 2AZ, UK
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We propose a quantum error correction protocol for continuous-variable finite-energy, approximate Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states undergoing small Gaussian random displacement errors, based on the scheme of Glancy and Knill [Phys. Rev. A 73, 012325 (2006)]. We show that combining multiple rounds of error-syndrome extraction with Bayesian estimation offers enhanced protection of GKP-encoded qubits over comparible single-round approaches. Furthermore, we show that the expected total displacement error incurred in multiple rounds of error followed by syndrome extraction is bounded by 2​π2\sqrt{\pi}. By recompiling the syndrome-extraction circuits, we show that all squeezing operations can be subsumed into auxiliary state preparation, reducing them to beamsplitter transformations and quadrature measurements.

I Introduction

Encoding and manipulating quantum information in continuous variable (CV) systems [1, 2, 3] is a promising route to realising a useful quantum computing device. Large scale CV cluster states can be generated on demand [4], and fast, high-quality one- and two-qubit Clifford gates are deterministically available [5]. Fault tolerant, measurement-based quantum computation is possible using CV cluster states along with CV measurements and non-Gaussian state injection  [6, 7], though the levels of squeezing required for fault tolerance are beyond the reach of current experiments [6, 8, 9, 10, 11].

A leading approach to CV quantum computation, proposed by Gottesman, Kitaev and Preskill [12], is based on the idea of encoding a qubit within an (infinite dimensional) oscillator. Ideal codeword wavefunctions within this paradigm correspond to infinite-energy Dirac combs, and are commonly referred to as GKP states. In practice, this ideal wavefunction is replaced by a finite-energy approximation, such as a comb of narrow Gaussian peaks modulated by a broad Gaussian envelope.

The appeal of GKP-encoded qubits is that they possess both an intrinsic robustness to physically motivated error channels and natural schemes for error syndrome extraction and correction. An initial proposal for GKP error correction was based on CV stabilizer generalisations of the Steane circuits [13] for error syndrome extraction. Subsequently, Glancy and Knill proposed a different method based on a beamsplitter transformation [14], which will provide the basis for the scheme detailed in this paper.

We define approximate GKP codewords with width Δ→=(Δ,κ)\vec{\Delta}=(\Delta,\kappa) as

ψμΔ→​(x)∝∑s∈ℤG1κ​[(2​s+μ)​π]​GΔ​[x−(2​s+μ)​π]\psi_{\mu}^{\vec{\Delta}}(x)\propto\sum_{s\in\mathbb{Z}}G_{\frac{1}{\kappa}}[(2s+\mu)\sqrt{\pi}\hskip 1.13791pt]\hskip 1.42271ptG_{\Delta}[x-(2s+\mu)\sqrt{\pi}\hskip 1.13791pt] (1)

where GΣ​(z)=exp⁡(−z22​Σ2)G_{\Sigma}(z)=\exp{(-\frac{z^{2}}{2\Sigma^{2}})} and μ∈{0,1}\mu\in\{0,1\} defines the logical basis states. Informally, for the logical 0 (1) state we have a superposition of Gaussians of width Δ\Delta centered at even (odd) values of π\sqrt{\pi}, with an overall Gaussian envelope of width 1/κ1/\kappa. Better approximations to the ideal GKP state are achieved with smaller values of Δ\Delta and κ\kappa, although these also correspond to larger average energy and an apparent increase in experimental difficulty.

Recently, Albert et al. [15] showed that the GKP code outperforms a number of other bosonic codes when states are exposed to amplitude damping and Gaussian random displacement errors. We will consider the latter, and write such an error acting on the state ρ^\hat{\rho} as

ℰσ0​(ρ^)=12​π​σ02​∫∫α∈ℂd2​α​Gσ0​(|α|)​D^​(α)​ρ^​D^​(α)†,\mathcal{E}_{\sigma_{0}}(\hat{\rho})=\frac{1}{2\pi\sigma_{0}^{2}}\displaystyle{\int\!\!\!\int\displaylimits_{\hskip-5.69046pt\alpha\in\mathbb{C}}}\!\!\hskip 5.69046pt\text{d}^{2}\alpha\hskip 5.69046ptG_{\sigma_{0}}(|\alpha|)\hskip 1.42271pt\hat{D}(\alpha)\hskip 1.42271pt\hat{\rho}\hskip 1.42271pt\hat{D}(\alpha)^{\dagger}\ , (2)

where the operator D^​(α)\hat{D}(\alpha) shifts the state in phase space by Re{α\alpha}, Im{α\alpha} in the q- and p-quadratures respectively, and the width σ0\sigma_{0} quantifies the extent of the error. Notably, this error model describes amplitude damping that is preceded by an offsetting pre-amplification [16], and it is therefore highly relevant to many experimental platforms. Despite this potential, explicit error correction protocols for accessible approximate states are currently lacking.

In this manuscript we present a new decoder for the GKP code undergoing Gaussian random displacement errors, based on the Glancy and Knill error recovery scheme and Bayesian estimation. In particular, we extend the scheme to enable enhanced error estimation using multiple syndrome extractions, enabling improved error supression which we show to be useful in extending the lifetime of states with a mean number of bosons as low as ten. We find that many rounds of syndrome extraction without active corrective displacement causes the qubit to drift in phase space by at most approximately 2​π2\sqrt{\pi} in each quadrature. Additionally, we recompile the syndrome extraction circuit in an experimentally friendly way, such that squeezing need only be applied to auxiliary states which can be prepared offline.

II Syndrome extraction

The GKP syndrome extraction scheme of Glancy and Knill  [14] can be broken down into two sequential circuits: q-SE and p-SE, which extract the error syndromes in the q- and p-quadrature respectively (see Fig. 1).

We begin our analysis with an arbitrary input qubit wavefunction QΔ→​(x)Q^{\vec{\Delta}}(x) that has undergone an unknown displacement error (u,v)(u,v)

QΔ→​(x)→(u,v)errorei​v​x​QΔ→​(x−u).Q^{\vec{\Delta}}(x)\xrightarrow[(u,v)]{\text{error}}\text{e}^{ivx}Q^{\vec{\Delta}}(x-u)\ . (3)

This corrupted qubit is input into the top mode of the q-SE circuit, while an auxiliary GKP state |ψ+Δ→⟩∝|ψ0Δ→⟩+|ψ1Δ→⟩\ket{\psi^{\vec{\Delta}}_{+}}\propto\ket{\psi^{\vec{\Delta}}_{0}}+\ket{\psi^{\vec{\Delta}}_{1}} is input into the bottom mode. The action of the q-SE circuit can be visualised in terms of the two-mode q-quadrature wavefunction. The beamsplitter B^π2\hat{B}_{\frac{\pi}{2}} causes an anticlockwise rotation by 45∘45^{\circ} in the joint quadrature space, and the subsequent squeezer S^2\hat{S}_{\sqrt{2}} scales the top-mode quadrature by 2\sqrt{2}. The error syndrome is then generated by a q-quadrature measurement of the auxiliary mode.

The p-SE circuit proceeds similarly, although there are subtle differences beyond a change of variables q→pq\rightarrow p, and squeezing in the conjugate direction (S^2→S^2†\hat{S}_{\sqrt{2}}\rightarrow\hat{S}^{\dagger}_{\sqrt{2}}). Indeed, we must also change the auxiliary state |ψ+Δ→⟩→|ψ0Δ→′⟩\ket{\psi_{+}^{\vec{\Delta}}}\rightarrow\ket{\psi_{0}^{\vec{\Delta}^{\prime}}} where Δ→′=(Δ/2,κ​2)\vec{\Delta}^{\prime}=(\Delta/\sqrt{2},\kappa\sqrt{2})—a departure from the proposal of Glancy and Knill, which we found necessary for sequential q-SE and p-SE circuits to be applied to approximate GKP states (see Appendix B for more details).

Following sequential q-SE and p-SE circuits, the qubit has transformed according to

ei​v​x​QΔ→​(x−u)→SEq-,p-ei​θ​(pm,v)​x​QΔ→​(x−θ⁡(xm,u))\text{e}^{ivx}Q^{\vec{\Delta}}(x-u)\xrightarrow[\text{SE}]{\text{q-,p-}}\text{e}^{i\theta(p_{\text{m}},v)x}Q^{\vec{\Delta}}\big(x-\theta(x_{\text{m}},u)\big)\ (4)

with a high fidelity (see Appendix D) when the displacement is small. Here, θ⁡(xm,u)\theta(x_{\text{m}},u) is given by

θ⁡(xm,u)=u2−fstep∗​(xm)\theta(x_{\text{m}},u)=\frac{u}{2}-f^{*}_{\text{step}}(x_{m}) (5)

where fstep∗​(xm)f^{*}_{\text{step}}(x_{m}) is the modified modular division by 4 function defined in Appendix A, and θ⁡(pm,v)\theta(p_{\text{m}},v) is defined similarly. These quantities can be interpreted as the total displacement experienced by the qubit: an unknown, random part u2\frac{u}{2} remaining from the error channel and a known part fstep∗​(xm)f^{*}_{\text{step}}(x_{m}) introduced by the measurement.

While an error correcting procedure could involve estimation of the total displacement θ⁡(xm,u)\theta(x_{m},u) and immediately applying a corrective displacement based on this estimate, we note that allowing an uncorrected qubit to undergo a further syndrome extraction process only results in another displaced version of the input qubit. With this in mind, our decoder uses measurement information from multiple rounds of errors and syndrome extraction without intermediate correction to estimate a single corrective displacement to apply. This memory-assisted approach is summarised in Fig. 2, alongside a contrasting memoryless approach which applies a correction after each syndrome extraction and then forgets about it.

We now proceed by extending our analysis from one round to multiple rounds of syndrome extraction. Say that after the hthh^{\text{th}} round of syndrome extraction we have histories of q-quadrature syndrome measurements x→m=(xm(1),…,xm(h))\vec{x}_{\mathrm{m}}=(x_{\mathrm{m}}^{(1)},\dotsc,x_{\mathrm{m}}^{(h)}) and displacement errors u→=(u1,…,uh)\vec{u}=(u_{1},\dotsc,u_{h}), and similarly p-quadrature values p→m=(pm(1),…,pm(h))\vec{p}_{\mathrm{m}}=(p_{\mathrm{m}}^{(1)},\dotsc,p_{\mathrm{m}}^{(h)}) and v→=(v1,…,vh)\vec{v}=(v_{1},\dotsc,v_{h}) for the p-quadrature. If each displacement error is small, then the input qubit is transformed according to

𝒳m(h)​(x→m)=xm(h)+12​∑j=1k−1[fstep∗​(𝒳m(j)​(x→m))2k−j−1]\mathcal{X}^{(h)}_{\text{m}}(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{m}})=x^{(h)}_{\text{m}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\Big[\frac{f_{\text{step}}^{*}\big(\mathcal{X}_{\text{m}}^{(j)}(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{m}})\big)}{2^{k-j-1}}\Big] (8)

It follows that the expected value for total displacement error in each quadrature after any number of syndrome extraction rounds is bounded above by approximately 2​π2\sqrt{\pi}.

In Fig. 2a, we identify a practical simplification to the combined q-SE, p-SE circuit that moves all squeezing operations offline onto auxiliary state preparation. To do so, we use a modified p-SE auxiliary state, S^2†​|ψ0Δ→′⟩\hat{S}^{\dagger}_{\sqrt{2}}\ket{\psi_{0}^{\vec{\Delta}^{\prime}}}, and reinterpret the p-quadrature measurement (pm→2​pmp_{\text{m}}\rightarrow\sqrt{2}p_{\text{m}}) (see Appendix F for proof).

III Decoder (Bayesian estimation)

We now show how to use the q- and p-SE measurement outcomes to estimate the final displacements when the loss channel is well characterised (i.e. σ0\sigma_{0} is known). For convenience, we set κ=Δ\kappa=\Delta in this section, although it is straightforward to extend the results to the more general case.

In the case of a single round of q-SE and p-SE application, the probability of measuring xmx_{\text{m}} given a shift error uu can be approximated as ℙ⁡(xm|u)∝ψ+Δ→​(2​xm−u)\mathbb{P}(x_{\text{m}}|u)\propto\psi^{\vec{\Delta}}_{+}(\sqrt{2}x_{\text{m}}-u), which we note is independent of both vv and pmp_{m}. By using a prior probability density function (PDF) corresponding to our characterised error channel and applying Bayes’ theorem, we obtain a posterior PDF

ℙ⁡(u|xm)∝ψ+Δ→​(2​xm−u)​e−u22​σ02.\mathbb{P}(u|x_{\text{m}})\propto\psi^{\vec{\Delta}}_{+}(\sqrt{2}x_{\text{m}}-u)\text{e}^{-\frac{u^{2}}{2\sigma_{0}^{2}}}. (9)

Assuming that Δ→\vec{\Delta} and σ0\sigma_{0} are both small compared to π\sqrt{\pi}, this posterior is well approximated by

ℙ⁡(u|xm)≈𝒩⁡(2​σ02​xm−π​σ02​⌊2​xmπ⌉Δ2+σ02,Δ2​σ02Δ2+σ02)\mathbb{P}(u|x_{\text{m}})\approx\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}\sigma_{0}^{2}x_{\text{m}}-\sqrt{\pi}\sigma_{0}^{2}\left\lfloor\frac{\sqrt{2}x_{\text{m}}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right\rceil}{\Delta^{2}+\sigma_{0}^{2}},\frac{\Delta^{2}\sigma_{0}^{2}}{\Delta^{2}+\sigma_{0}^{2}}\right) (10)

and we take our estimate u~\tilde{u} of the shift error uu to be the mean of this Gaussian. Explicitly,

u~=2​σ02​xm−π​σ02​⌊2​xmπ⌉Δ2+σ02,\tilde{u}=\frac{\sqrt{2}\sigma_{0}^{2}x_{\text{m}}-\sqrt{\pi}\sigma_{0}^{2}\left\lfloor\frac{\sqrt{2}x_{\text{m}}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right\rceil}{\Delta^{2}+\sigma_{0}^{2}}, (11)

which is a good approximation of the minimum mean square error (MMSE) estimator for uu. The estimate for the displacement required to counteract the acquired error is therefore θ⁡(xm,u~)\theta(x_{\text{m}},\tilde{u}), from combining equations (5) and (11).

The corresponding p-quadrature conditional probabilities can be obtained by substituting (u,xm,Δ)→(v,pm,2​Δ)(u,x_{\text{m}},\Delta)\rightarrow(v,p_{\text{m}},2\Delta), where the asymmetry between the q- and p-quadrature originates from the differing widths of the auxiliary states.

For multiple rounds, the estimation of the cumulative unknown displacement caused by the vector u→\vec{u} is achieved in the same spirit as estimating the parameter uu in the single round case, except with a messier-looking (although, still efficiently computable) estimator.

The probability of obtaining the q-quadrature measurement outcome xm(h)x_{\text{m}}^{(h)} in the hthh^{\text{th}} round, given the measurement values obtained in the previous (h−1)(h-1) rounds and displacement shifts in all hh rounds, is ℙ⁡(xm(h)|u1,…,uh,xm(1),…,xm(h−1))∝ψ+Δ→​(2​xm(h)−𝒰h)\mathbb{P}(x^{(h)}_{\text{m}}|u_{1},...,u_{h},x^{(1)}_{\text{m}},...,x^{(h-1)}_{\text{m}})\propto\psi^{\vec{\Delta}}_{+}(\sqrt{2}x^{(h)}_{\text{m}}-\mathcal{U}_{h}). Here, 𝒰h\mathcal{U}_{h} is the shift contributed in the hthh^{\text{th}} round by the error channel, transformed to account for all previous steps (see Appendix A for an explicit definition). We now apply Bayes’ theorem with Gaussian prior PDFs for the error in each of MM rounds, resulting in the posterior PDF

ℙM(q)​(u→|x→m)∝∏h=1Mψ+Δ→​(2​xm(h)−𝒰h)⋅Gσ0​(uh),\mathbb{P}^{(\text{q})}_{M}\left(\vec{u}\big|\vec{x}_{\text{m}}\right)\propto\prod_{h=1}^{M}\psi^{\vec{\Delta}}_{+}\left(\sqrt{2}x^{(h)}_{\text{m}}-\mathcal{U}_{h}\right)\cdot\hskip 1.42271ptG_{\sigma_{0}}\left(u_{h}\right)\ , (12)

The quantity that we actually wish to estimate is θMerr​(u→)\theta_{M}^{\mathrm{err}}(\vec{u}) from equation (7), which is a linear combination of elements from u→\vec{u}. The corresponding PDF is given by

with ak=2−(M+1−k)a_{k}=2^{-(M+1-k)} and

As in the single round case, the posterior mean is used as the MMSE estimator for the displacement error. We see that the posterior is well approximated by a Gaussian with a mean a→⋅u~→\vec{a}\cdot\vec{\tilde{u}} which can be calculated directly from syndrome measurement results. An explicit approach to this calculation is presented as an algorithm in Appendix E.

Also of interest is the variance of this Gaussian, a→T⋅Σ⋅a→\vec{a}^{\hskip 1.42271pt\text{T}}\hskip-1.42271pt\cdot\Sigma\cdot\vec{a}, as it corresponds to the uncertainty in our estimation. In Appendix C we show that, if σ0Δ<12\frac{\sigma_{0}}{\Delta}<\frac{1}{2} (which is true for all M>1M>1), the variance converges to

Vq​(M)=σ023[(1−4−M)+(σ0Δ)249(4−2​M+3(1+2M)4−M−4)],\begin{split}V_{\text{q}}(M)&=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}}{3}\Big[(1-4^{-M})\\ &+\Big(\frac{\sigma_{0}}{\Delta}\Big)^{2}\frac{4}{9}\big(4^{-2M}+3(1+2M)4^{-M}-4\big)\Big],\end{split} (15)

neglecting terms within the bracket of order (σ0Δ)4\big(\frac{\sigma_{0}}{\Delta}\big)^{4} and higher. Note that Vq→σ023V_{\text{q}}\rightarrow\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}}{3} very quickly as MM grows, given that σ0Δ≪1\frac{\sigma_{0}}{\Delta}\ll 1.

IV Numerical results

The aim of a quantum error correction (QEC) procedure is to protect logical quantum information. Pantaleoni et al. recently reported a method to extract logical information from approximate GKP states [17]. In essence, this reduces a density matrix function describing a CV state to a qubit density matrix (ρ^CV→ρ^qubit\hat{\rho}^{\text{CV}}\rightarrow\hat{\rho}^{\text{qubit}}). Using this, fidelities between qubit density matrices at the input and output of an error correction procedure can be computed in order to benchmark its performance.

In Fig. 3 we present the results of numerical simulations for the specific case of a GKP code with Δ≈0.22\Delta\approx 0.22 (corresponding to an average number of bosons n¯≈10\bar{n}\approx 10). For varying numbers of rounds of error channel application followed by syndrome extraction, we benchmark error correction with our memory-assisted decoder against density matrix function simulations of the memoryless decoder and no error correction at all.

We observe that error correction is improved by using our memory-assisted decoder instead of the memoryless decoder — a finding similar to that of Vuillot et al. [18] and Noh et al. [9] for Steane-based GKP syndrome extraction. Note that Δ\Delta is large enough that the memoryless decoder performs worse than no QEC once a few hundred rounds are considered. We also see that the quality of the memory-assisted error corrected state is higher than the uncorrected state, despite the state containing a low average number of bosons. Furthermore, the fidelity of the input state is approximately preserved through application of the memory-assisted error correction scheme.

V Summary and outlook

We have described an explicit protocol for GKP quantum error correction that provides improved protection from Gaussian displacement errors with reduced experimental requirements. Notably, we have shown that GKP states undergo a total displacement (and therefore require a correction) that is approximately bounded by 2​π2\sqrt{\pi} in each quadrature, after multiple rounds of error syndrome extraction. A memory-assisted decoder based on Bayesian estimation was developed to specify the near-optimal corrective displacement, and numerical simulations have shown that this results in significantly improved error correction compared to a memoryless decoder when applied to an approximate GKP state with a small average number of bosons.

Recent experiments have demonstrated GKP states encoded in oscillations of trapped ions [10] and microwave fields of superconducting resonators [11]. In the latter case, states are shown with widths of (Δ,κ)=(0.16,0.32)(\Delta,\kappa)=(0.16,0.32). As these values are similar to those we have studied here, this suggests that our decoder can be exploited by near-term experiments as part of an error correction procedure. Additionally, the Glancy-Knill syndrome extraction circuit at the core of our method may be better suited to realistic devices than the more studied SUM gate syndrome extraction, since the latter requires more gates, and therefore more physical components, to implement [19].

The error model that we have considered in this work also pertains to errors that arise in teleporting a GKP state along a CV cluster state with finite squeezing [20]. In this situation, the finite squeezing of the cluster state induces a displacement error. We anticipate that it will therefore be possible to apply our error correction scheme between nodes on a CV cluster state graph, and thereby lower the squeezing threshold for universal fault tolerant quantum computation using CV cluster states and GKP state injection.

Data availability statement

This is a theoretical paper and there is no experimental data available beyond the numerical simulation data described in the paper. Kwok Ho Wan performed all numerical experiments, all the authors contributed to the manuscript and the project was supervised by Alex Neville and Steve Kolthammer.

    ψμΔ→​(x)=Nμ​∑s∈ℤG1κ​[(2​s+μ)​π]​GΔ​[x−(2​s+μ)​π].\psi_{\mu}^{\vec{\Delta}}(x)=N_{\mu}\sum_{s\in\mathbb{Z}}G_{\frac{1}{\kappa}}[(2s+\mu)\sqrt{\pi}\hskip 1.13791pt]\hskip 0.85355ptG_{\Delta}[x-(2s+\mu)\sqrt{\pi}\hskip 0.56917pt]. (16)

Appendix B Single-Round Error Estimation

Here we present further details for a single round of syndrome extraction (SE) and error estimation.

B.1 Wavefunction after the q-SE circuit

First, we show that the state after the q-SE circuit is approximated by simple transformation of its initial wavefunction.

Theorem 1.

A q-SE circuit with measurement result xmx_{\mathrm{m}} approximately transforms an input qubit wavefunction according to

QαΔ→​(x−u)→Qs⁡(xm)+α2Δ′→​(x−u2).Q_{\alpha}^{\vec{\Delta}}(x-u)\rightarrow Q_{s(x_{\mathrm{m}})+\frac{\alpha}{2}}^{\vec{\Delta^{\prime}}}\big(x-\frac{u}{2}\big).
Proof.

The two-mode input to the q-SE circuit has the wavefunction

Φin​(x,y)=QαΔ→​(x−u)⋅ψ+Δ→​(y),\Phi_{\mathrm{in}}(x,y)=Q_{\alpha}^{\vec{\Delta}}(x-u)\cdot\psi_{+}^{\vec{\Delta}}(y), (19)

where the qubit QαΔ→=a0​ψ0+αΔ→+a1​ψ1+αΔ→Q_{\alpha}^{\vec{\Delta}}=a_{0}\psi_{0+\alpha}^{\vec{\Delta}}+a_{1}\psi_{1+\alpha}^{\vec{\Delta}} has an error shift uu and relative peak shift α\alpha.

After the beam-splitter and squeezer of the q-SE circuit, the wavefunction is

Φ⁡(x,y)=QαΔ→​(x+y2−u)⋅ψ+Δ→​(−x+y2),\Phi(x,y)=Q_{\alpha}^{\vec{\Delta}}(x+\frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}-u)\cdot\psi_{+}^{\vec{\Delta}}(-x+\frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}), (20)

which may be expanded as

Φ(x,y)=∑μ,n,maμ​Nμ​G1κ​[(2​n+μ+α)​π]⋅GΔ​[x−u+y2−(2​n+μ+α)​π]⋅G1κ​(m​π)⋅GΔ​(−x+y2−m​π),\begin{split}\Phi(x,y)=\sum_{\mu,n,m}&a_{\mu}N_{\mu}G_{\frac{1}{\kappa}}[(2n+\mu+\alpha)\sqrt{\pi}\hskip 1.13791pt]\\ &\cdot G_{\Delta}[x-u+\frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}-(2n+\mu+\alpha)\sqrt{\pi}\hskip 1.13791pt]\\ &\cdot G_{\frac{1}{\kappa}}(m\sqrt{\pi}\hskip 1.13791pt)\cdot\hskip 1.42271ptG_{\Delta}(-x+\frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}-m\sqrt{\pi}\hskip 1.13791pt),\end{split} (21)

where the sums are for integer n,mn,m and μ∈{0,1}\mu\in\{0,1\}.

We now identify that this may be written in terms of un-rotated GKP wavefunctions. To do so, we regroup Gaussian functions of the same width by completing the square in the exponent, resulting in

Φ⁡(x,y)∝∑βψβ+α2Δ→′​(y2−u2)⋅(a0​ψβ+α2Δ→′​(x−u2)+a1​ψ1+β+α2Δ→′​(x−u2))\begin{split}\Phi(x,y)&\propto\sum_{\beta}\psi_{\beta+\frac{\alpha}{2}}^{\vec{\Delta}^{\prime}}\Big(\frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{u}{2}\Big)\\ &\cdot\Big(a_{0}\psi_{\beta+\frac{\alpha}{2}}^{\vec{\Delta}^{\prime}}\big(x-\frac{u}{2}\big)+a_{1}\psi_{1+\beta+\frac{\alpha}{2}}^{\vec{\Delta}^{\prime}}\big(x-\frac{u}{2}\big)\Big)\end{split} (22)

where the sum is over β∈{−12,0,12,1}\beta\in\{-\frac{1}{2},0,\frac{1}{2},1\}. This wavefunction is a superposition of two-mode GKP states with relative peaks shifts differing by β\beta. Note also that the initial error uu is now shared equally by the modes. To simplify the expression, we have used the approximation that the normalization constants are equal: 1N0≈N0N12≈N0N1/2N−1/2\frac{1}{N_{0}}\approx\frac{N_{0}}{N_{1}^{2}}\approx\frac{N_{0}}{N_{1/2}N_{-1/2}}.

For a measurement result xmx_{\mathrm{m}}, the output wavefunction is proportional to Φ⁡(x,xm)\Phi(x,x_{\mathrm{m}}). For a particular xmx_{\mathrm{m}}, one term from equation (22) is much larger than the others, since the weighting functions are positive-valued and nearly orthogonal if Δ\Delta is sufficiently smaller than π/2\sqrt{\pi}/2. The dominant term is given by β=s⁡(xm−u2−α​π2)\beta=s(x_{\mathrm{m}}-\frac{u}{\sqrt{2}}-\alpha\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}), and therefore we approximate that the output state as that given by the most likely case u=0u=0.

The average fidelity of this approximation is given by the average value of |ψs⁡(xm)+α2Δ→′|2|\psi_{s(x_{\mathrm{m}})+\frac{\alpha}{2}}^{\vec{\Delta}^{\prime}}|^{2} taken over the joint probability distribution ℙ⁡(xm,u)=ℙ⁡(xm|u)​ℙ​(u)\mathbb{P}(x_{\mathrm{m}},u)=\mathbb{P}(x_{\mathrm{m}}|u)\mathbb{P}(u) (these distributions are discussed below). ∎

A similar result is obtained for the p-quadrature syndrome extraction. In this case, however, the widths undergo the inverse transformation according to (Δ,κ)→(Δ​2,κ/2)(\Delta,\kappa)\rightarrow(\Delta\sqrt{2},\kappa/\sqrt{2}). Appropriately designed q-SE and p-SE steps can therefore be used sequentially to prevent any overall change in the widths. In particular, we begin with a q-SE step using a qubit and auxiliary state of width (Δ,κ)(\Delta,\kappa). The following p-SE step then uses an auxiliary state of width (Δ/2,κ/2)(\Delta/\sqrt{2},\kappa/\sqrt{2}), and the final state from this has the same width as the initial one. We note that the effect of width reduction through syndrome extraction cannot be observed in the Δ=0\Delta=0 unphysical states calculation.

B.2 Wavefunction after error, q-SE and p-SE

We now extend the above calculation to include a subsequent p-SE step. In particular, we will show the transformation of the input state is well approximated by

QΔ→​(x−u)​ei​v​x→QΔ→​(x−θ⁡(xm,u))​ei​θ​(pm,v)​xQ^{\vec{\Delta}}(x-u)\text{e}^{ivx}\rightarrow Q^{\vec{\Delta}}\big(x-\theta(x_{\mathrm{m}},u)\big)\text{e}^{i\theta(p_{\mathrm{m}},v)x}\hskip 2.84544pt\, (23)

where the shift function θ\theta is defined as

θ⁡(y,b)=b/2−fstep∗​(y).\theta(y,b)=b/2-f^{*}_{\mathrm{step}}(y). (24)

The two-mode state after the p-SE beam-splitter and squeezer is given by

Φ⁡(x,z)=ei⁡(x2+z2)​v⋅ψ0Δ′→​(x2−z2)⋅QΔ′→​(x2+z2−u2−fstep∗​(xm−u/2)),\begin{split}\Phi(x,z)=\hskip 2.84544pt&\text{e}^{i(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}})v}\cdot\psi^{\vec{\Delta^{\prime}}}_{0}\Big(\frac{x}{2}-\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}\Big)\\ &\cdot Q^{\vec{\Delta^{\prime}}}\Big(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{u}{\sqrt{2}}-f^{*}_{\mathrm{step}}(x_{\mathrm{m}}-u/\sqrt{2})\Big)\ ,\end{split} (25)

where the quadrature zz corresponds to the mode to be measured. This p-quadrature measurement is achieved using the Fourier transform of the two-mode wavefunction

ℱ{Φ(x,z)}=ℱy→p−pm2{ψΔ′→0(y)}⋅ℱw→p+pm2​{ei​w​v​QΔ′→​(w−u2+fstep∗​(xm−u/2))}.\begin{split}\mathcal{F}\big\{\Phi&(x,z)\big\}=\hskip 2.84544pt\mathcal{F}_{y\rightarrow p-\frac{p_{\text{m}}}{\sqrt{2}}}\Big\{\psi^{\vec{\Delta^{\prime}}}_{0}(y)\Big\}\\ &\cdot\mathcal{F}_{w\rightarrow p+\frac{p_{\text{m}}}{\sqrt{2}}}\Big\{\text{e}^{iwv}Q^{\vec{\Delta^{\prime}}}\big(w-\frac{u}{\sqrt{2}}+f^{*}_{\text{step}}(x_{\mathrm{m}}-u/\sqrt{2})\Big)\big\}.\end{split} (26)

where the transform is taken for variables (x,z)→(p,pm)(x,z)\rightarrow(p,p_{\text{m}}), and on the right hand side we use the change of variables w=x2+z2w=\frac{x}{2}+\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}} and y=x2−z2y=\frac{x}{2}-\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}. The shift property of the transform yields

Φ~​(p,pm)=ψ~0Δ′→​(p−pm2)​Q~0Δ′→​(p+pm2−v)⋅e−i​p​(u/2−fstep∗​(xm−u/2))\begin{split}\tilde{\Phi}(p,p_{\mathrm{m}})=&\tilde{\psi}^{\vec{\Delta^{\prime}}}_{0}(p-\frac{p_{\mathrm{m}}}{\sqrt{2}})\tilde{Q}^{\vec{\Delta^{\prime}}}_{0}(p+\frac{p_{\mathrm{m}}}{\sqrt{2}}-v)\\ &\cdot\text{e}^{-ip(u/2-f^{*}_{\text{step}}(x_{\mathrm{m}}-u/\sqrt{2}))}\end{split} (27)

where we denote Fourier transforms as g~=ℱ​{g}\tilde{g}=\mathcal{F}\{g\}.

Since the finite-energy GKP states are approximate eigenstates of the Fourier transform, the first two terms are similar to the product of two rotated GKP states, treated above. Using similar methods, we find the approximate relationship

ψ~0Δ′→​(p−pm2)⋅Q~Δ′→​(p+pm2−v)∝Q~Δ→​(p−v2+fstep∗​(pm−v/2)).\begin{split}\tilde{\psi}^{\vec{\Delta^{\prime}}}_{0}\Big(p-\frac{p_{\text{m}}}{\sqrt{2}}\Big)&\cdot\tilde{Q}^{\vec{\Delta^{\prime}}}\Big(p+\frac{p_{\text{m}}}{\sqrt{2}}-v\Big)\\ &\propto\tilde{Q}^{\vec{\Delta}}\Big(p-\frac{v}{2}+f^{*}_{\mathrm{step}}(p_{\mathrm{m}}-v/\sqrt{2})\Big).\end{split} (28)

We now simplify the step function by noting that fstep∗​(pm−v/2)≈fstep∗​(pm)f^{*}_{\mathrm{step}}(p_{\mathrm{m}}-v/\sqrt{2})\approx f^{*}_{\mathrm{step}}(p_{\mathrm{m}}). The success probability of this approximation will be discussed later. Finally, we take the inverse Fourier transform to find the desired result given by equation (23).

B.3 Bayesian estimation of the q-quadrature error

In order to estimate the unknown shift error, we wish to determine its posterior probability distribution. To do so, we use the prior probability distribution, specified by the error model, and a likelihood function ℙ⁡(xm|u)\mathbb{P}(x_{\text{m}}|u) that we now calculate from the wavefunction.

Theorem 2.

The probability of measurement result xmx_{\mathrm{m}} from a q-SE circuit with initial state ψαΔ→​(x−u)\psi^{\vec{\Delta}}_{\alpha}(x-u) is

ℙ⁡(xm|u)∝ψ+Δ→​(2​xm−u).\mathbb{P}(x_{\mathrm{m}}|u)\propto\psi^{\vec{\Delta}}_{+}(\sqrt{2}x_{\mathrm{m}}-u).
Proof.

We start with the two-mode wavefunction given in equation (22). The probability for measurement result xmx_{\mathrm{m}} is

ℙ⁡(xm|u)=∫x∈ℝ|Φ⁡(x,xm)|2​𝑑x≈∑β|ψβΔ→′​(xm2−u2)|2,\begin{split}\mathbb{P}(x_{\text{m}}|u)&=\int_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\big|\Phi(x,x_{\mathrm{m}})\big|^{2}dx\\ &\approx\sum_{\beta}\Big|\psi_{\beta}^{\vec{\Delta}^{\prime}}\Big(\frac{x_{\text{m}}}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{u}{2}\Big)\Big|^{2},\end{split} (29)

where in the second step we neglect overlap of the GKP wavefunctions to approximate |∑ψβ|2≈∑|ψβ|2|\sum\psi_{\beta}|^{2}\approx\sum|\psi_{\beta}|^{2}.

An alternate expression is obtained from the relationships

∑β∈{0,1}\displaystyle\sum_{\beta\in\{0,1\}} |ψβΔ→′​(xm2−u2)|2∝ψ0Δ→​(0)​ψ0Δ→​(2​xm−u)\displaystyle\Big|\psi_{\beta}^{\vec{\Delta}^{\prime}}\Big(\frac{x_{\text{m}}}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{u}{2}\Big)\Big|^{2}\propto\psi_{0}^{\vec{\Delta}}(0)\psi_{0}^{\vec{\Delta}}\Big(\sqrt{2}x_{\text{m}}-u\Big) (30)
∑β∈{±12}\displaystyle\sum_{\beta\in\{\pm\frac{1}{2}\}} |ψβΔ→′​(xm2−u2)|2∝ψ0Δ→​(0)​ψ1Δ→​(2​xm−u),\displaystyle\Big|\psi_{\beta}^{\vec{\Delta}^{\prime}}\Big(\frac{x_{\text{m}}}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{u}{2}\Big)\Big|^{2}\propto\psi_{0}^{\vec{\Delta}}(0)\psi_{1}^{\vec{\Delta}}\Big(\sqrt{2}x_{\text{m}}-u\Big),

which may be shown by re-indexing akin to the derivation of equation (28). Addition of these two equations yields the desired result. ∎

Using Bayes’ theorem, the posterior probability distribution is

ℙ⁡(u|xm)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(u|x_{\text{m}}) ∝ℙ⁡(xm|u)​ℙ​(u)\displaystyle\propto\mathbb{P}(x_{\text{m}}|u)\mathbb{P}(u) (31)
∝ψ+Δ→​(2​xm−u)​e−u22​σ02,\displaystyle\propto\psi^{\vec{\Delta}}_{+}(\sqrt{2}x_{\text{m}}-u)\text{e}^{-\frac{u^{2}}{2\sigma_{0}^{2}}},

where in the last step we have explicitly written the Gaussian error model. The unknown shift can now be estimated from equation (31) using an appropriate estimator, such as the mean of ℙ⁡(u|xm)\mathbb{P}(u|x_{\text{m}}). For a given xmx_{\text{m}}, along with Δ≪π\Delta\ll\sqrt{\pi} and u≪1u\ll 1, ℙ⁡(u|xm)\mathbb{P}(u|x_{\text{m}}) can be well approximated by a normal distribution

ℙ⁡(u|xm)≈𝒩⁡(2​σ02​xm−π​σ02​⌊2​xmπ⌉Δ2+σ02,Δ2​σ02Δ2+σ02).\mathbb{P}(u|x_{\text{m}})\approx\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}\sigma_{0}^{2}x_{\text{m}}-\sqrt{\pi}\sigma_{0}^{2}\left\lfloor\frac{\sqrt{2}x_{\text{m}}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right\rceil}{\Delta^{2}+\sigma_{0}^{2}},\frac{\Delta^{2}\sigma_{0}^{2}}{\Delta^{2}+\sigma_{0}^{2}}\right)\ . (32)

The approximation of the posterior as a normal distribution given reasonable parameter choices is an important step used below in multi-round calculations.

B.4 Bayesian estimation of q- and p-quadrature error

We now expand on the previous section to estimate an unknown shift in both quadratures.

Theorem 3.

The probability of measurement results xmx_{\text{m}} and pmp_{\text{m}} from sequential q-SE and p-SE circuits with an initial state ei​v​x​ψαΔ→​(x−u)\mathrm{e}^{ivx}\psi_{\alpha}^{\vec{\Delta}}(x-u) is

ℙ(xm,pm|u,v)∝ψ+Δ→(2xm−u)⋅ψ+(2​Δ,κ/2)(2pm−v).\mathbb{P}(x_{\mathrm{m}},p_{\mathrm{m}}|u,v)\propto\psi^{\vec{\Delta}}_{+}(\sqrt{2}x_{\text{m}}-u)\cdot\psi^{(2\Delta,\kappa/2)}_{+}(\sqrt{2}p_{\text{m}}-v)\ .
Proof.

Starting from the wavefunction in equation (22), the probability of pmp_{\mathrm{m}} is

ℙ⁡(pm|u,v,xm)=∫p∈ℝ|Φ~​(p,pm)|2​𝑑p∝ψ+(2​Δ,κ/2)​(2​pm−v),\begin{split}\mathbb{P}(p_{\text{m}}|u,v,x_{\mathrm{m}})&=\int_{p\in\mathbb{R}}\big|\tilde{\Phi}(p,p_{\mathrm{m}})\big|^{2}\ dp\\ &\propto\psi^{(2\Delta,\kappa/2)}_{+}(\sqrt{2}p_{\text{m}}-v),\end{split} (33)

where the second step follows by analogy to equations (20-22) and (33-30). The desired result follows from the relationship of conditional probabilities ℙ(xm,pm|u,v)=ℙ(xm|u,v)ℙ(pm|u,v,xm)\mathbb{P}(x_{\mathrm{m}},p_{\mathrm{m}}|u,v)=\mathbb{P}(x_{\mathrm{m}}|u,v)\mathbb{P}(p_{\mathrm{m}}|u,v,x_{\mathrm{m}}). ∎

Note that ℙ⁡(pm|u,v,xm)\mathbb{P}(p_{\mathrm{m}}|u,v,x_{\mathrm{m}}) is independent of xmx_{\mathrm{m}} and uu. We can therefore write ℙ(xm,pm|u,v)=ℙ(xm|u)ℙ(pm|v)\mathbb{P}(x_{\mathrm{m}},p_{\mathrm{m}}|u,v)=\mathbb{P}(x_{\mathrm{m}}|u)\mathbb{P}(p_{\mathrm{m}}|v) where the ℙ⁡(pm|v)\mathbb{P}(p_{\mathrm{m}}|v) differs from ℙ⁡(xm|u)\mathbb{P}(x_{\mathrm{m}}|u) according to the transformation Δ→2​Δ,κ→κ/2\Delta\rightarrow 2\Delta,\kappa\rightarrow\kappa/2.

Appendix C Multi-Round Error Estimation

We now consider MM rounds of error followed by q-SE and p-SE circuits, with an aim to estimate the shift error on the final state.

Wavefunction after multiple rounds

As shown for the single-round scenario, the wavefunction after each round is a shifted version of the input. An expression for the shift after each round is calculated iteratively. After round hh, with a history of measurements x→m=(xm(1),…,xm(h))\vec{x}_{\mathrm{m}}=(x_{\mathrm{m}}^{(1)},\dotsc,x_{\mathrm{m}}^{(h)}) and shift errors u→=(u1,…,uh)\vec{u}=(u_{1},\dotsc,u_{h}), the total q-shift is

θh​(x→m,u→)=∑k=1h12h−k​θ​(𝒳k​(x→m),uk),\theta_{h}\big(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{m}},\vec{u}\big)=\sum_{k=1}^{h}\frac{1}{2^{h-k}}\theta\big(\mathcal{X}_{k}(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{m}}),u_{k}\big), (34)

where θ\theta is defined in equation (24) and

𝒳m(k)​(x→m)=xm(k)+12​∑j=1k−1[fstep∗​(𝒳m(j)​(x→m))2k−j−1]\mathcal{X}^{(k)}_{\text{m}}(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{m}})=x^{(k)}_{\text{m}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\Big[\frac{f_{\text{step}}^{*}\big(\mathcal{X}_{\text{m}}^{(j)}(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{m}})\big)}{2^{k-j-1}}\Big] (35)

for h>1h>1, and 𝒳m(1)=xm(1)\mathcal{X}^{(1)}_{\text{m}}=x^{(1)}_{\text{m}}. The parameter 𝒳m(k)\mathcal{X}^{(k)}_{\text{m}} can be interpreted as the measurement outcome xm(k)x^{(k)}_{\text{m}} transformed to account for previous measurement-induced shifts.

Equation (34) can also be expanded as

θh​(x→m,u→)=∑j=1h[uk2h−j+1]−∑k=1h[fstep∗​(𝒳m(k)​(x→m))2h−k]=θherr​(u→)−θhstep​(x→m),\begin{split}\theta_{h}\big(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{m}},\vec{u}\big)&=\sum_{j=1}^{h}\Big[\frac{u_{k}}{2^{h-j+1}}\Big]-\sum_{k=1}^{h}\Big[\frac{f_{\text{step}}^{*}\big(\mathcal{X}_{\text{m}}^{(k)}(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{m}})\big)}{2^{h-k}}\Big]\\ &=\theta_{h}^{\mathrm{err}}(\vec{u})-\theta_{h}^{\mathrm{step}}(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{m}}),\end{split} (36)

which identifies the total shift as comprised of a known measurement-induced shift θhstep​(x→m)\theta_{h}^{\mathrm{step}}(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{m}}) and the accumulation of unknown error θherr​(u→)\theta_{h}^{\mathrm{err}}(\vec{u}). The aim of our error estimation after MM rounds is to use x→m\vec{x}_{\mathrm{m}} to estimate θMerr​(u→)\theta_{M}^{\mathrm{err}}(\vec{u}).

An analogous approach to the p-shifts leads to the wavefunction

ei​θh​(p→m,v→)​x​QΔ→​(x−θh​(x→m,u→))\text{e}^{i\theta_{h}(\vec{p}_{\mathrm{m}},\vec{v})x}Q^{\vec{\Delta}}\big(x-\theta_{h}(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{m}},\vec{u})\big) (37)

after hh rounds, for an initial qubit state QΔ→​(x)Q^{\vec{\Delta}}(x). This is assuming that fstepf_{\text{step}} is independent of uku_{k}, which is true if fstep∗​(xm)=fstep∗​(xm−u/2)f_{\text{step}}^{*}(x_{\text{m}})=f_{\text{step}}^{*}(x_{\text{m}}-u/\sqrt{2}). We shall discuss the error of such an approximation in a later section.

C.1 Total qubit drift

Without active corrective shift at each round of QEC, the magnitude of the total drift of the state in phase space can be bounded. Using the fact that |fstep∗|≤π|f_{\text{step}}^{*}|\leq\sqrt{\pi} and taking the variance of each the error shifts to be σ02\sigma_{0}^{2}, an application of the triangle inequality gives:

|θ⁡(xm(h),𝒰h)|,|θ⁡(pm(h),𝒱h)|≤2​π(1−2−h)+|𝒩⁡(0,σ02​(1−4−h)3)|,\begin{split}|\theta(x_{\text{m}}^{(h)},\mathcal{U}_{h})|\hskip 2.84544pt,\hskip 2.84544pt|\theta(p_{\text{m}}^{(h)},\mathcal{V}_{h})|\leq 2\sqrt{\pi}&(1-2^{-h})\\ &+\Big|\mathcal{N}\Big(0,\sigma_{0}^{2}\frac{(1-4^{-h})}{3}\Big)\Big|\ ,\end{split} (38)

where 𝒩⁡(μ,V)\mathcal{N}(\mu,V) is a Gaussian random variable with mean μ\mu and Variance VV. The quantities 1−4−h1-4^{-h} and 1−2−h1-2^{-h} converge very quickly to 1 as hh increases, meaning that for multiple rounds we have

|θ⁡(xm(h),𝒰h)|,|θ⁡(pm(h),𝒱h)|≤2​π+|𝒩⁡(0,σ023)|.|\theta(x_{\text{m}}^{(h)},\mathcal{U}_{h})|\hskip 2.84544pt,\hskip 2.84544pt|\theta(p_{\text{m}}^{(h)},\mathcal{V}_{h})|\leq 2\sqrt{\pi}+\Big|\mathcal{N}\Big(0,\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}}{3}\Big)\Big|\ . (39)

This means that even without active error corrective shift after each round of syndrome extraction, the GKP qubit is expected to drift by a maximum of 2​π2\sqrt{\pi} in phase space along with some Gaussian random variable with variance σ02/3\sigma_{0}^{2}/3 in the worst case scenario. Consequently, the energy of the physical system is not divergent if we extend the QEC for many rounds, if errors are sufficiently small at each round.

C.2 Memory-assisted decoder

The probability distributions for the xx and pp measurement values obtained in the hthh^{\text{th}} round, given all the previous measurement results and displacement shifts, are given by expressions similar in spirit to that in Theorem 2:

ℙ⁡(xm(h)|u1,…,uh,xm(1),…,xm(h−1))∝ψ+(Δ,Δ)​(2​xm(h)−𝒰h)ℙ⁡(pm(h)|v1,…,vh,pm(1),…,pm(h−1))∝ψ+(2​Δ,Δ/2)​(2​pm(h)−𝒱h).\begin{split}&\mathbb{P}(x^{(h)}_{\text{m}}|u_{1},...,u_{h},x^{(1)}_{\text{m}},...,x^{(h-1)}_{\text{m}})\propto\psi^{(\Delta,\Delta)}_{+}(\sqrt{2}x^{(h)}_{\text{m}}-\mathcal{U}_{h})\\ &\mathbb{P}(p^{(h)}_{\text{m}}|v_{1},...,v_{h},p^{(1)}_{\text{m}},...,p^{(h-1)}_{\text{m}})\propto\psi^{(2\Delta,\Delta/2)}_{+}(\sqrt{2}p^{(h)}_{\text{m}}-\mathcal{V}_{h}).\end{split} (40)

Using Bayes’ Theorem to flip these distributions, for MM rounds we obtain

ℙM(u→,v→|x→m,p→m)=ℙ(q)M(u→|x→m)⋅ℙ(p)M(v→|p→m)ℙM(q)​(u→|x→m)∝∏h=1Mψ+Δ→​(2​xm(h)−𝒰h)⋅Gσ0​(uh)ℙM(p)​(v→|p→m)∝∏h=1Mψ+(2​Δ,Δ/2)​(2​pm(h)−𝒱h)⋅Gσ0​(vh).\begin{split}\mathbb{P}_{M}(\vec{u},\vec{v}|\vec{x}_{\text{m}},\vec{p}_{\text{m}})=\mathbb{P}^{(\text{q})}_{M}(\vec{u}|\vec{x}_{\text{m}})\cdot\hskip 1.42271pt\mathbb{P}^{(\text{p})}_{M}(\vec{v}|\vec{p}_{\text{m}})\\ \mathbb{P}^{(\text{q})}_{M}(\vec{u}|\vec{x}_{\text{m}})\propto\prod_{h=1}^{M}\psi^{\vec{\Delta}}_{+}(\sqrt{2}x^{(h)}_{\text{m}}-\mathcal{U}_{h})\cdot\hskip 1.42271ptG_{\sigma_{0}}(u_{h})\\ \mathbb{P}^{(\text{p})}_{M}(\vec{v}|\vec{p}_{\text{m}})\propto\prod_{h=1}^{M}\psi^{(2\Delta,\Delta/2)}_{+}(\sqrt{2}p^{(h)}_{\text{m}}-\mathcal{V}_{h})\cdot\hskip 1.42271ptG_{\sigma_{0}}(v_{h}).\end{split} (41)

We can see that the q- and p-quadratures equations have the similar forms and can be unchangeable (q↔pq\leftrightarrow p) if u↔vu\leftrightarrow v, xm↔pmx_{\text{m}}\leftrightarrow p_{\text{m}} and (Δ,κ)↔(2​Δ,κ/2)(\Delta,\kappa)\leftrightarrow(2\Delta,\kappa/2), so we will focus on the q-quadature version for now. The PDF for u→\vec{u} is well approximated by a multivariate Gaussian distribution, a step known as Laplace’s approximation in statistics, which we write as

ℙM(q)​(u→|x→m)≈𝒩⁡(u~→,Σ),\mathbb{P}^{(\text{q})}_{M}(\vec{u}|\vec{x}_{\text{m}})\approx\mathcal{N}(\vec{\tilde{u}},\Sigma)\ , (42)

for mean vector u~→\vec{\tilde{u}} and covariance matrix Σ\Sigma.

We derive the inverse of the covariance matrix, Σ−1\Sigma^{-1}, exactly by completing the square of the exponents of the Gaussians in equation (42):

(Σ−1)α,β=(δα,βσ02+1Δ2​∑h=mα,βM14h​2−(α+β)),mα,β=max⁡{α,β}.\begin{split}&(\Sigma^{-1})_{\alpha,\beta}=\Big(\frac{\delta_{\alpha,\beta}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}}+\frac{1}{\Delta^{2}}{\displaystyle\sum_{h=m_{\alpha,\beta}}^{M}\frac{1}{4^{h}2^{-(\alpha+\beta)}}}\Big)\ ,\\ &m_{\alpha,\beta}=\max{\{\alpha,\beta\}}\ .\end{split} (43)

To derive u~→\vec{\tilde{u}} via completing the square, we need to invert the matrix Σ−1\Sigma^{-1}. It’s generally hard to invert a M×MM\times M symmetric matrix for an arbitrary M, but we can approximate the covariance matrix via a Neumann series expansion of the matrices, under the assumption of small displacements. We find the covariance matrix has components

Σα,β≈σ02​δα,β−σ04Δ2​∑h=mα,βM14h​2−(α+β)+𝒪⁡(σ06Δ4),\Sigma_{\alpha,\beta}\approx\sigma_{0}^{2}\hskip 1.42271pt\delta_{\alpha,\beta}-\frac{\sigma_{0}^{4}}{\Delta^{2}}\sum_{h=\text{m}_{\alpha,\beta}}^{M}\frac{1}{4^{h}2^{-(\alpha+\beta)}}+\mathcal{O}\Big(\frac{\sigma_{0}^{6}}{\Delta^{4}}\Big)\ , (44)

and note that this Neumann series converges if σ0Δ<12\frac{\sigma_{0}}{\Delta}<\frac{1}{2} (which works for all MM). By ignoring from order 𝒪⁡(σ06Δ6)\mathcal{O}\Big(\frac{\sigma_{0}^{6}}{\Delta^{6}}\Big) upwards in the expansion, we compute

u~k=(σ0Δ)2{2k​∑j=1MFj2j−(σ0Δ)2∑h=1M[(∑n=mk,hM2k+h4n)(∑j=hMFj2j)]2h},\begin{split}\tilde{u}_{k}=\Big(\frac{\sigma_{0}}{\Delta}\Big)^{2}\Bigg\{&2^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\frac{F_{j}}{2^{j}}\\ &-\Big(\frac{\sigma_{0}}{\Delta}\Big)^{2}\sum_{h=1}^{M}\Big[\Big(\hskip-5.69046pt\sum_{n=\text{m}_{k,h}}^{M}\hskip-5.69046pt\frac{2^{k+h}}{4^{n}}\Big)\Big(\sum_{j=h}^{M}\frac{F_{j}}{2^{j}}\Big)\Big]2^{h}\Bigg\}\ ,\end{split} (45)

where mk,h=max​{k,h}\text{m}_{k,h}=\text{max}\{k,h\} and Fh=2​𝒳m(h)−π​⌊2​𝒳m(h)/π⌉F_{h}=\sqrt{2}\mathcal{X}_{\text{m}}^{(h)}-\sqrt{\pi}\left\lfloor\sqrt{2}\mathcal{X}_{\text{m}}^{(h)}/\sqrt{\pi}\right\rceil, which is equation (14) in the main text.

Now that we have characterised the multivariate Gaussian noise model (multivariate due to many rounds) by its covariance matrix, we wish to estimate the random part of the total displacement after MM rounds, given by ∑k=1Muk/2M−k+1\sum_{k=1}^{M}u_{k}/2^{M-k+1}. The corresponding PDF is

ℙ⁡(∑k=1Muk2M−k+1|x→m)=𝒩⁡(a→⋅u~→,a→T⋅Σ⋅a→),\mathbb{P}\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{M}\frac{u_{k}}{2^{M-k+1}}\Big|\vec{x}_{\text{m}}\Big)=\mathcal{N}(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{\tilde{u}}\ ,\ \vec{a}^{\hskip 1.42271pt\text{T}}\hskip-1.42271pt\cdot\Sigma\cdot\vec{a})\ , (46)

with ak=2−(M+1−k)a_{k}=2^{-(M+1-k)}.

We use the mean of this posterior distribution as the MMSE estimator, with uncertainty given by the variance

Vq=Var​(∑k=1Muk2M−k+1)=a→T⋅Σ⋅a→.V_{\text{q}}=\text{Var}\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{M}\frac{u_{k}}{2^{M-k+1}}\Big)=\vec{a}^{\hskip 1.42271pt\text{T}}\hskip-1.42271pt\cdot\Sigma\cdot\vec{a}. (47)

Neglecting terms of order (σ06Δ4)\big(\frac{\sigma_{0}^{6}}{\Delta^{4}}\big) and higher, we compute

Vq​(M)=σ023[(1−4−M)+(2​σ03​Δ)2(4−2​M+3(1+2M)4−M−4)].\begin{split}V_{\text{q}}(M)=&\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}}{3}\Big[(1-4^{-M})+\\ &\Big(\frac{2\sigma_{0}}{3\Delta}\Big)^{2}(4^{-2M}+3(1+2M)4^{-M}-4)\Big]\ .\end{split} (48)

We can see that Vq→σ023V_{\text{q}}\rightarrow\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}}{3}, very quickly as MM grows. Note that using measurement results from all rounds of syndrome measurements allows the error to be estimated more precisely than is achievable otherwise.

Appendix D Approximations and qubit fidelity

In our calculations, two significant approximations are made in expressing the qubit wavefunction emerging from a syndrome extraction circuit as a displacement of the incoming wavefunction. For the single-round case, these were discussed following equation (22). First, in identifying the dominant GKP-like term in the resulting wavefunction, we approximate that fstep∗​(xm−u/2)=fstep∗​(xm)f_{\text{step}}^{*}(x_{\text{m}}-u/\sqrt{2})=f_{\text{step}}^{*}(x_{\text{m}}). Second, we keep only the dominant term in the sum of equation (22). Each of these approximations reduce the fidelity of our description of the final state.

D.1 Tracking error

Unlikely measurement outcomes and unusually large displacement errors can cause an incorrect identification of the dominant GKP-like term, which we refer to as a tracking error. In this section, we estimate the probability that our description of the state after one or multiple rounds of syndrome extraction, as given in equation 37, does not contain a tracking error.

D.1.1 Single round

For a single round, the joint probability density function of xmx_{\text{m}} and uu is

ℙ⁡(u,xm)=C​∑n∈ℤG1/Δ​(n​π)​GΔ​(2​xm−u−n​π)​Gσ0​(u).\mathbb{P}(u,x_{\text{m}})=C\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}G_{1/\Delta}(n\sqrt{\pi})G_{\Delta}(\sqrt{2}x_{\text{m}}-u-n\sqrt{\pi})G_{\sigma_{0}}(u)\ . (49)

No tracking error occurs if xmx_{\text{m}} and uu are in the region 𝒮\mathcal{S} for which |fstep∗​(xm)−fstep∗​(xm−u/2)|=0|f_{\text{step}}^{*}(x_{\text{m}})-f_{\text{step}}^{*}(x_{\text{m}}-u/\sqrt{2})|=0.

We therefore define the success probability for one round and error width σ0\sigma_{0} to be

Ptracksucc​(1,σ0)=∫Sℙ⁡(u,xm)​d​𝒮,P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{track}}(1,\sigma_{0})=\int_{S}\mathbb{P}(u,x_{\text{m}})\text{d}\mathcal{S}\ , (50)

for which the integration region could be re-written as xm∈ℝx_{\text{m}}\in\mathbb{R} and u∈𝒯u\in\mathcal{T}, where 𝒯=[−π,0]+2​mod​(x−π2/2,π2)\mathcal{T}=[-\sqrt{\pi},0]+\sqrt{2}\text{mod}(x-\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}/2,\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}). The normalisation constant C=[2πσ0ΔΘ3(0,e−πΔ2/2)]−1C=[\sqrt{2}\pi\sigma_{0}\Delta\Theta_{3}(0,\text{e}^{-\pi\Delta^{2}/2})]^{-1}, where Θ3\Theta_{3} is the Jacobi-Theta function of the third kind.

For our example in the main text where (Δ,σ02)=(0.2182,0.0005)(\Delta,\sigma_{0}^{2})=(0.2182,0.0005), we calculate 1−Ptracksucc​(1,σ)≈1×10−111-P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{track}}(1,\sigma)\approx 1\times 10^{-11}.

D.1.2 Multiple rounds

For multiple rounds, the joint probability density function of x→m\vec{x}_{\text{m}} and u→\vec{u} is

ℙ⁡(u→,x→m)=∏h=1Mψ+Δ→​(2​xm(h)−𝒰h)⋅Gσ0​(uh)\mathbb{P}(\vec{u},\vec{x}_{\text{m}})=\prod_{h=1}^{M}\psi^{\vec{\Delta}}_{+}(\sqrt{2}x^{(h)}_{\text{m}}-\mathcal{U}_{h})\cdot\hskip 1.42271ptG_{\sigma_{0}}(u_{h}) (51)

Similar to the single round case, the probability for MM successful rounds is given by

Ptracksucc​(M,σ0)=∫ℒℙ⁡(u→,x→m)​d​ℒ,P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{track}}(M,\sigma_{0})=\int_{\mathcal{L}}\mathbb{P}(\vec{u},\vec{x}_{\text{m}})\text{d}\mathcal{L}\ , (52)

where ℒ\mathcal{L} is the region defined by fstep∗​(𝒳m(j))=fstep∗​(xm(j)−𝒰j/2)f^{*}_{\text{step}}(\mathcal{X}^{(j)}_{\text{m}})=f^{*}_{\text{step}}(x^{(j)}_{\text{m}}-\mathcal{U}_{j}/\sqrt{2}), ∀1<j<M\forall 1<j<M.

This calculation is simplified by changing variables to 𝒳→\vec{\mathcal{X}} and 𝕌→\vec{\mathbb{U}}, where 𝕌h=∑k=1uk2h−k\displaystyle\mathbb{U}_{h}=\sum_{k=1}\frac{u_{k}}{2^{h-k}} for h>1h>1 and 𝕌1=u1\mathbb{U}_{1}=u_{1}, which leads to

Psucctrack(M,OPENσ0)>∫ℒ∏h=2M[ψ+Δ→​(2​𝒳m(h)−𝕌h)⋅G2​σ05​(𝕌h)]⋅ψ+Δ→​(2​𝒳m(1)−𝕌1)⋅Gσ0​(𝕌h)⋅dM​𝒳→​dM​𝕌→.\begin{split}P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{track}}(M,&\sigma_{0})>\int_{\mathcal{L}}\prod_{h=2}^{M}\Big[\psi^{\vec{\Delta}}_{+}(\sqrt{2}\mathcal{X}^{(h)}_{\text{m}}-\mathbb{U}_{h})\hskip 1.42271pt\cdot G_{\frac{2\sigma_{0}}{\sqrt{5}}}(\mathbb{U}_{h})\Big]\\ &\cdot\psi^{\vec{\Delta}}_{+}(\sqrt{2}\mathcal{X}^{(1)}_{\text{m}}-\mathbb{U}_{1})\cdot\hskip 1.42271ptG_{\sigma_{0}}(\mathbb{U}_{h})\cdot\text{d}^{M}\hskip-1.42271pt\vec{\mathcal{X}}\hskip 1.42271pt\text{d}^{M}\vec{\mathbb{U}}\ .\end{split} (53)

Note the multidimensional integral is now separated into a product of single integrals over the integration regions fstep∗​(𝒳m(j))=fstep∗​(𝒳m(j)−𝕌j/2)f^{*}_{\text{step}}(\mathcal{X}^{(j)}_{\text{m}})=f^{*}_{\text{step}}({\mathcal{X}^{(j)}_{\text{m}}-\mathbb{U}_{j}/\sqrt{2}}) for all 2<j<M2<j<M. A convenient bound lower bound can be written in terms of single-round probabilities

Ptracksucc​(M,σ0)>[Ptracksucc​(1,2​σ05)]M.P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{track}}(M,\sigma_{0})>\Big[P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{track}}\Big(1,\frac{2\sigma_{0}}{\sqrt{5}}\Big)\Big]^{M}. (54)

For (Δ,σ02)=(0.2182,0.0005)(\Delta,\sigma_{0}^{2})=(0.2182,0.0005) and M=200M=200, we calculate 1−Ptracksucc​(M,σ0)≈2×10−91-P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{track}}(M,\sigma_{0})\approx 2\times 10^{-9}.

D.2 Truncation error

In order to iterate the single-round calculation to describe multiple rounds, we approximate the sum in equation 22 by its single dominant term. The total probability associated with neglected terms gives a bound on the fidelity of our truncated-state description, which we refer to as the truncation error.

D.2.1 Single round

The wavefunction emerging from single syndrome extraction circuit, described by equation 22, can be expressed in ket notation as

|Φ⁡(x|u,xm)⟩=R⁡(u,xm)​∑γψγΔ→′​(xm2−u2)​|QγΔ→⟩,\ket{\Phi(x|u,x_{\text{m}})}=R(u,x_{\text{m}})\sum_{\gamma}\psi_{\gamma}^{\vec{\Delta}^{\prime}}\Big(\frac{x_{\text{m}}}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{u}{2}\Big)\ket{Q_{\gamma}^{\vec{\Delta}}}\ , (55)

where R⁡(u,xm)R(u,x_{\text{m}}) is a normalisation constant. We note the dominant term as |QβΔ→⟩\ket{Q_{\beta}^{\vec{\Delta}}} and calculate its amplitude

A⁡(β)=R⁡(u,xm)​∑γψγΔ→′​(xm2−u2)​⟨QβΔ→|QγΔ→⟩.A(\beta)=R(u,x_{\text{m}})\sum_{\gamma}\psi_{\gamma}^{\vec{\Delta}^{\prime}}\Big(\frac{x_{\text{m}}}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{u}{2}\Big)\braket{Q_{\beta}^{\vec{\Delta}}|Q_{\gamma}^{\vec{\Delta}}}\ . (56)

The average success of the truncated description is given by

Ptruncsucc​(1,σ0)=∫all space|A⁡(β)|2​ℙ​(u,xm)​d​u​d​xm.P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{trunc}}(1,\sigma_{0})=\int_{\text{all\ space}}\hskip-22.76228pt|A(\beta)|^{2}\mathbb{P}(u,x_{\text{m}})\ \text{d}u\hskip 1.42271pt\text{d}x_{\text{m}}. (57)

For the example (Δ,σ02)=(0.2182,0.0005)(\Delta,\sigma_{0}^{2})=(0.2182,0.0005), we calculate 1−Ptruncsucc​(1,σ0)≈1×10−131-P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{trunc}}(1,\sigma_{0})\approx 1\times 10^{-13}.

D.2.2 Multiple rounds

Similarly, we estimate a success probability after MM rounds as

Ptruncsucc​(M,σ0)=∏h=1M∫∑βh|A⁡(βh)|2​Gσ0​(uh)⋅ψ+Δ→​(2​xm(h)−𝒰h)​d​u→​d​x→m.\begin{split}P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{trunc}}(M,\sigma_{0})=&\prod_{h=1}^{M}\int\sum_{\beta_{h}}|A(\beta_{h})|^{2}G_{\sigma_{0}}(u_{h})\hskip 1.42271pt\\ &\cdot\psi^{\vec{\Delta}}_{+}(\sqrt{2}x^{(h)}_{\text{m}}-\mathcal{U}_{h})\ \text{d}\vec{u}\hskip 1.42271pt\text{d}\vec{x}_{\text{m}}\ .\end{split} (58)

As in equation 54, we bound the multi-round probability in terms of the single-round expression

Ptruncsucc​(M,σ0)>(Ptruncsucc​(1,2​σ0/5))M.P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{trunc}}(M,\sigma_{0})>(P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{trunc}}(1,2\sigma_{0}/\sqrt{5}))^{M}\ . (59)

For (Δ,σ02)=(0.2182,0.0005)(\Delta,\sigma_{0}^{2})=(0.2182,0.0005) and M=200M=200 we calculate 1−Ptruncsucc​(M,σ0)≈2×10−111-P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{trunc}}(M,\sigma_{0})\approx 2\times 10^{-11}.

D.3 Syndrome error

In addition to causing a truncation error in the final state description, the neglected portion of the wavefunction might also cause a misleading measurement outcome at any round of syndrome extraction. We assume that such a measurement would cause an incorrect identification akin to a tracking error and refer to this as a syndrome error.

The probability that a syndrome error is avoided in round kk is given by Ptruncsucc​(k,σ0)P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{trunc}}(k,\sigma_{0}). Using equation 59, the success probability after MM rounds is thus

Psynsucc​(M,σ0)=∏k=1MPtruncsucc​(k,σ0)>(Ptruncsucc​(1,2​σ0/5))M⁡(M+1)/2.\begin{split}P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{syn}}(M,\sigma_{0})&=\prod_{k=1}^{M}P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{trunc}}(k,\sigma_{0})\\ &>(P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{trunc}}(1,2\sigma_{0}/\sqrt{5}))^{M(M+1)/2}.\end{split} (60)

For (Δ,σ02)=(0.2182,0.0005)(\Delta,\sigma_{0}^{2})=(0.2182,0.0005) and M=200M=200 we calculate 1−Psynsucc​(M,σ0)≈5×10−91-P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{syn}}(M,\sigma_{0})\approx 5\times 10^{-9}.

D.4 Total error and state fidelity

To estimate a final qubit fidelity, as in the example shown in Fig. 3, we first calculate the fidelity FρF_{\rho} from the output state described by our Bayesian estimation procedure, following the approach of Pantaleoni et al. [17]. We then assume that a tracking, truncation or syndrome error results in a complete depolarized qubit with probability upper-bounded by 1−Ptotalsucc1-P^{\text{succ}}_{\text{total}}. A lower bound on the final qubit fidelity is therefore given by F=(Fρ−12)​Psucc+12F=(F_{\rho}-\frac{1}{2})P^{\text{succ}}+\frac{1}{2}.

Appendix E Pseudocode for Error Estimation

After MM rounds of syndrome extraction, as depicted in Fig. 2c, our results can be used to estimated the random contribution of the total displacement error from measurement results x→m\vec{x}_{\text{m}} and p→m\vec{p}_{\text{m}}. Algorithm D.4 gives an explicit description of this calculation for the q-quadrature.

Appendix F Offline Squeezing Derivation

A diagrammatic derivation of the offline squeezing circuit is shown in FIG. 4. Starting with the Glancy-Knill syndrome extraction circuits, we recompile and re-interpret measurement results to obtain a circuit in which the qubit state interacts only with 50:50 beamsplitters.
